title: Chapter 17 — That The Aspect Of Society In The United States Is At Once Excited And Monotonous
paragraphs: Nothing, it would seem, could be better suited to stimulate and feed curiosity than the spectacle of the United States. Fortunes, opinions, and laws are in constant variation there. It is as if immutable nature herself were mutable, so great are the changes wrought on her by the hand of man. Yet in the end the sight of this excited community becomes monotonous, and after watching the moving pageant for a while the spectator grows tired of it. Among aristocratic nations every man is pretty nearly stationary in his own sphere, but men are astonishingly unlike each other—their passions, their notions, their habits, and their tastes are essentially different. Nothing changes, but everything differs. In democracies, by contrast, all men are alike and do things pretty much alike. It is true that they are subject to great and frequent vicissitudes, but since the same events of good or bad fortune keep recurring, only the name of the actors changes—the play is always the same. The aspect of American society is animated, because men and things are always changing; but it is monotonous, because all these changes are alike.

Men living in democratic ages have many passions, but most of their passions either end in the love of riches or proceed from it. The reason for this is not that their souls are narrower, but that the importance of money is really greater in such times. When all the members of a community are independent of, or indifferent to, each other, the cooperation of each can only be obtained by paying for it. This infinitely multiplies the purposes to which wealth can be put, and increases its value. When the reverence that belonged to what is old has vanished, birth, condition, and profession no longer distinguish men, or scarcely do so. Hardly anything but money remains to create strongly marked differences between them, and to raise some of them above the common level. The distinction that comes from wealth is increased by the disappearance or diminution of all other distinctions. Among aristocratic nations money reaches only a few points on the vast circle of human desires; in democracies it seems to lead to everything. The love of wealth can therefore be traced, either as a principal or accessory motive, at the bottom of everything Americans do. This gives all their passions a sort of family resemblance, and soon makes the survey of them extremely tiresome. The perpetual recurrence of the same passion is monotonous; the particular methods by which this passion seeks its own gratification are no less so.

In an orderly and constituted democracy like the United States, where men cannot enrich themselves by war, by public office, or by political confiscation, the love of wealth drives them mainly into business and manufacturing. Although these pursuits often produce great upheavals and disasters, they cannot prosper without strictly regular habits and a long routine of small, uniform acts. The stronger the passion is, the more regular the habits, and the more uniform the acts. It might be said that it is the intensity of their desires that makes Americans so methodical: it agitates their minds, but it disciplines their lives.

The remark I apply here to America can be extended to almost all of our contemporaries. Variety is disappearing from the human race; the same ways of acting, thinking, and feeling are to be met with all over the world. This is not only because nations act more upon each other and are more faithful in their mutual imitation; it is also because, as the men of each country abandon more and more the peculiar opinions and feelings of a caste, a profession, or a family, they simultaneously arrive at something closer to the constitution of man, which is everywhere the same. Thus they become more alike, even without having imitated each other. Like travelers scattered across some great forest crisscrossed by paths that all converge on a single point: if every one of them keeps his eyes fixed on that point and advances toward it, they insensibly draw nearer together—though they do not seek, do not see, do not even know each other—and in the end they will be astonished to find themselves all collected on the same spot. All nations that take, not any particular man, but man himself as the object of their research and imitation, are tending in the end toward a similar state of society, like these travelers converging on the central clearing of the forest.
